patterns.title: Build a Web of Goals
patterns.short_description: Connect recurring activities through shared benefits so they support several purposes with less conflict.
use_when: Each worthwhile goal seems to need a separate competing commitment.
An activity advances one purpose while undermining another.
You want to understand how recurring activities support one another.
One expected payoff carries the entire value of a pursuit.
goals: Find several worthwhile contributions in a manageable activity
Connect activities through shared purposes and applicable skills
Keep costs, conflicts, and failed expectations visible
Adapt activities as their contributions become clearer
mechanisms: Map intended benefits and unwanted side effects
Represent goals as shared nodes and activities as modules
Choose compatible arrangements rather than proliferating separate programs
Reconsider an activity when a contribution changes without assuming all value is lost
not_ideal_when: Combining purposes removes something essential supplied by a specialist activity.
Benefits are asserted without checking actual costs or experience.
Every leisure activity is being forced to justify itself through productivity.
Shared dependencies are being mistaken for guaranteed resilience.
example_user_queries: Every new goal seems to add another obligation to my week.
Can fewer activities support more of what matters to me?
My efforts to improve one part of life make another part harder.
How do I see which commitments support one another?
Could my hobbies, friendships, and practical learning fit together better?
An activity did not deliver one expected benefit; is it still worth doing?
I want a diagram of how my activities connect to my goals.
I keep paying for separate solutions to problems that might be connected.
How can I reduce conflict between saving money and enjoying life?
How do I keep several reasons for a pursuit without making every hobby useful?
What side effects should I include when planning a change?
My whole plan depends on a single payoff working out.

figures.question: How do three activities join through shared goals?
figures.mapping: Each labeled point is a goal. Each shaded polygon is a recurring activity. Shapes share points; neither edges nor geometry encode causation or measured magnitude.
figures.phone_composition: The same graph is arranged vertically with larger labels. Node membership and activity identity remain unchanged.

figures.question: What remains when one expected benefit does not occur?
figures.mapping: A three-goal cooking module is compared with the same module after the expense benefit fails. Dashed links and a crossed-out node denote the unavailable benefit; connection and skills remain possible reasons to continue.
figures.changed: The lower-expenses expectation is unsupported in the worked month.
figures.phone_composition: The two comparison panels stack with the same node identities and states.

visual.concept_graphic: Three triangular activity modules join through shared goal points; the purple module bridges the two ink modules.
visual.provenance: Original editable SVG geometry and examples, inspired by the goal/activity encoding in the supplied book excerpt; no traced or reproduced book figures.

sources.title: Jacob Lund Fisker, Early Retirement Extreme
sources.basis: Nine user-supplied screenshot excerpts, especially A web of goals and Tensegrity; no page numbers visible.
sources.supports: Effects beyond a primary goal, activity modules joined at shared goals, and adaptive value when one purpose changes.

sources.title: Jacob Lund Fisker, About ERE
sources.supports: Author's description of mutually supportive skills and adaptive web-of-goals contingency planning.

patterns.evidence_boundary: An educational adaptation of the supplied framework. Tensegrity is treated as a metaphor, not a proved resilience property. Examples make no causal, medical, financial-return, or universally superior lifestyle claims.
